reading.body:
AMD is a California public company founded in 1969 with one registered MCP server and no listed products or cases.

The only concrete operational fact here is a single MCP entry, ai.lamdis/exchange, described as paying people nearby for physical work such as verifying whether something is true or having a task done. That is a marketplace for human labor, not a chip or a data center. Nothing in the data connects AMD to compute supply, buildings, or power, so the record cannot support any claim about AMD's role in AI infrastructure.

The law exposure field is a count of 281 tied to California, which places the company's legal footprint in one jurisdiction without saying what the exposure consists of. The profile gives a ticker, a founding year, a headquarters, and a website. Products and cases are both empty arrays, so the absence of listed hardware is a gap in the record, not evidence that none exists.

What this does not tell the reader is anything about AMD's actual business, its fabrication partners, its power contracts, or its data center footprint. A reader looking for the compute layer will not find it here. The data covers identity and one tool registration, and stops there.

profile_text.body:
AMD is a public company founded in 1969 and headquartered in Santa Clara, California, and it trades under the ticker AMD. On its own site, the company describes itself as delivering high-performance and adaptive computing solutions for data center AI, AI PCs, intelligent edge devices, gaming, and beyond. It says it is the only AI partner offering CPU, GPU, and adaptive computing solutions, and it emphasizes open standards, co-innovation, and end-to-end AI deployment across the data center, edge, and end user.

The site describes several AI efforts. AMD Ross is described as an agentic AI assistant spanning software, silicon, and board design to accelerate embedded system design, optimization, debug, and deployment. The company says an acquisition brought leading AI model research expertise to AMD to help shape future AI infrastructure and strengthen the open AI ecosystem. It also points to locally-run AI models on PCs, a resource hub for AI developers, and a video series in which Mark Papermaster and Mike Clark discuss the evolution of the Zen x86 architecture and the role of CPUs in AI.

The site states that AMD has operations in California, where it is recorded with 281 cases. An MCP server listed as ai.lamdis/exchange is associated with the company, described as a way to pay people nearby for physical work, such as finding out if something is true or having it done.
